newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tax shortfall to push Germany over EMU limit - poll.
newsitem.headline: Tax shortfall to push Germany over EMU limit - poll.

text.p: The German government is expected to find itself 16 billion marks out of pocket on Thursday when the tax estimates for 1997 are released, the average of forecasts in a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.

Most economists polled -- some expecting the gap to be as much as 20 billion marks -- are united in their prediction that the hole in the government's account will push Germany over the deficit limit target laid down in the Maastricht treaty for European economic and monetary union.
But most also think Finance Minister Theo Waigel will announce a petrol tax rise in an effort to raise extra cash and reduce the deficit.

Of 10 economists asked, five predict the tax projection will show a 15 billion mark shortfall, two expect a 20 billion gap, while two more are forecasting a shortfall of 17 and 18 billion respectively.
Only one analyst, Nikolaus Keis at Bayerische Vereinsbank in Munich, thinks the government will be only 10 billion marks down, in line with Bonn's own prediction.

The estimates, due for release on Thursday, will take centre stage in German political circles and financial markets with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government desperate to shave its budget deficit to qualify for EMU, due to start in 1999.

Ulrike Kastens, economist at Trinkhaus Capital Management (TCM) in Duesseldorf expected a 17 billion mark shortfall. Taking this figure into consideration, Germany's 1997 deficit was likely to be 3.2 percent of GDP, sparking a new debate on possible EMU delay.
"The debate concerning the on-schedule commencement of EMU is likely to intensify," TCM said.
Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt is more pessimistic, expecting a 1997 deficit ratio of 3.4 percent, even though he expects the tax gap to be slightly less -- 15 billion marks.

Waigel has already said further measures will have to be taken to meet the government's target for a 2.9 percent 1997 deficit/GDP ratio, warning that tax revenues will show a shortfall of around eight to 10 billion marks from estimates made last November.
The finance minister said he intended to pursue spending cuts rather than tax increases to generate extra cash, adding that a complete freeze on new spending cannot be ruled out.
But only three of the economists polled said they expected no tax rises, with the remaining 70 percent predicting a rise in petrol tax.

Some economists have said a 15 to 20 pfennig rise per litre could be on the way, saying such a move would be politically less painful for Kohl since German inflation is comfortably below the Bundesbank's medium-term two percent target.
A few analysts, however, said markets may well be relieved on Thursday after weeks of gloomy predictions.
"Our view is that a positive surprise is much more probable," analysts at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said in a research note.
"We assume that the working group will come to the conclusion that tax revenues will be only eight to nine billion marks lower than the figure projected back in November."
With this forecast, the analysts said Thursday's data would serve to "banish all remaining doubts" about Germany's ability to meet the Maastricht criteria and about EMU starting on time.
